Speculative decoding is a technique designed to accelerate the speed of large language model (LLM) inference without altering the final output. To understand why it works, you must first recognize the primary bottleneck in text generation: autoregressive decoding. Currently, most LLMs generate text one token at a time. For each new token, the model must process the entire context window, including all previously generated tokens, to calculate the probability distribution for the next one. This sequential process is computationally expensive and slow, as it requires a full forward pass through the model for every single character or word added to the output.

Speculative decoding solves this by introducing a "draft" model. This smaller, faster model runs in parallel with the main, larger model. The draft model quickly predicts a sequence of future tokens, often several at a time, based on the current context. It does not wait for the main model to finish; it simply guesses what the main model is likely to produce next.

The main model then takes this draft sequence and verifies it in a single, parallel pass. Instead of checking one token at a time, the main model evaluates the entire proposed sequence simultaneously. If the main model agrees with the draft model’s prediction for a token, that token is accepted and added to the final output. If it disagrees, the draft model’s prediction is rejected, and the process restarts from that point.

The key to this method’s efficiency is that the main model’s verification step is often much faster than generating the tokens sequentially. Even if the draft model is wrong, the main model can reject the incorrect part quickly. More importantly, if the draft model is correct—which is frequently the case for predictable text—the main model can accept multiple tokens at once. This effectively bypasses the need for multiple sequential forward passes.

Crucially, this does not change what the model would have written. The final output is determined entirely by the main model’s probability distribution. The draft model only suggests; the main model decides. Therefore, the quality and content of the text remain identical to standard autoregressive decoding. The speedup comes from reducing the number of times the heavy main model has to perform a full sequential pass, replacing it with a combination of a fast draft and a parallel verification step. This makes speculative decoding a powerful tool for improving latency in real-time applications without sacrificing accuracy.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# --- Argument validation ---------------------------------------------------
if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <directory>" >&2
    exit 1
fi

dir="$1"

if [[ ! -d "$dir" ]]; then
    echo "Error: '$dir' is not a directory" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# --- Find, compress, and count ---------------------------------------------
count=0

# -f  : find files only
# -name: match *.log
# -mmin: older than 7 days (7*24*60 minutes)
# -print0: null-delimited output to handle spaces/special chars safely
# -print0 | xargs -0: pass null-delimited list to gzip
# -n  : gzip will print nothing on success; we count via wc
#
# We use a while-read loop with process substitution to be fully safe
# with spaces, newlines, and other special characters in filenames.

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    gzip --no-clobber "$file"
    ((count++))
done < <(find "$dir" -type f -name '*.log' -mmin +43200 -print0)

echo "$count"
```

| `gzip --no-clobber "$file"` | Compress in-place. `--no-clobber` prevents overwriting an existing `.gz` (avoids a silent data-loss scenario). |

When two different keys compute to the same index in a hash table's underlying array, the map has to decide how to deal with that overlap. There are two fundamental strategies. The first is called chaining, in which each slot in the array holds not just a single entry but rather a small linked list or another compact container of entries. When a collision occurs, the new key-value pair is simply appended to that slot's internal collection, and lookups later scan through it linearly. The second strategy is open addressing, where instead of growing the bucket, the map simply keeps looking for the next available empty slot by following a small deterministic offset pattern. In the simplest form, it just checks the next index, then the one after that, wrapping around to the beginning of the array if necessary. More sophisticated schemes, such as double hashing, use a second hash function to vary the step size, which tends to spread entries out more evenly and avoids long consecutive runs. Either way, the point is to preserve the overall O(1) average-case behavior: as long as the table isn't too full, collisions remain rare and these small per-collision costs don't add up to anything noticeable.

Resizing is what keeps things from ever getting "too full." Each hash map tracks a threshold, typically expressed as a load factor—the ratio of the number of elements currently stored to the size of the underlying array. When inserting an element pushes that ratio past the configured limit (often around 0.75 for many standard implementations, though it can be tuned), the map allocates a new internal array, almost always twice the previous capacity, and then rehashes every existing entry into the enlarged array. This rehashing step recomputes each key's index in the new, larger table, which spreads the entries out so that collision probability drops again. The old array is then discarded, its memory reclaimed, and the map's internal bookkeeping—capacity, size, load factor threshold, and so on—is updated accordingly. On the other end of the spectrum, some implementations also shrink the array when the load factor falls well below a certain floor (perhaps 0.25 or 0.3), to avoid wastefully holding onto a much larger-than-needed buffer after many deletions. The resizing itself is a transient O(n) operation that touches every element, which is why it's deferred until necessary rather than checked on every single access; it amortizes out to constant time across a sequence of inserts.

plain.content:
When two different keys happen to produce the same hash value, the hash map has to figure out where to store both of them, since a hash table is ultimately just an array of fixed-size slots indexed by that hash. The most common strategy for handling this is called chaining. In this approach, each slot in the underlying array doesn't actually hold a single key-value pair; instead, it holds the head of a small list (or some equivalent linked structure) of pairs. Every time a new key maps to an already occupied slot, it simply gets appended to that list. When you look up a key, you first compute its hash, jump to the corresponding slot, and then walk through whatever list happens to live there until you find a matching key or reach the end. This keeps lookups fast on average because the lists are expected to remain very short, but in a degenerate worst case — where many keys all collide into the same slot — you've effectively turned a fast operation into a linear scan, which is the main performance risk the whole design is trying to avoid.

The other major collision-handling technique, sometimes called open addressing, works differently. Rather than keeping a list at each slot, you keep the table as a flat array where each slot holds at most one pair. When a collision is detected, you apply some deterministic probing sequence to find the next available slot — for instance, checking slot plus one, then slot plus two, and so on (linear probing), or using a more varied offset pattern to reduce clustering. The downside here is that you can't just delete a pair from its slot and be done; you have to mark it as tombstoned, and even then, insertions and deletions interact in subtle ways that require careful handling to avoid breaking the probing sequence. Chaining is more forgiving and easier to reason about, while open addressing tends to be more cache-friendly because everything lives in one contiguous block of memory, which is why some implementations favor it despite the slightly more complex bookkeeping.

Resizing comes into play when the table gets too full relative to its capacity. Most implementations track something called a load factor, which is essentially the ratio of actual stored entries to total available slots, and they set a threshold — often something like zero seventy-five or zero eighty — that triggers a resize. The reason for this threshold rather than waiting until the array is completely full is that as the table fills up, collisions and, in the open-addressing case, clustering get progressively worse, and lookup and insertion times creep up in a way that compounds across many operations. It's cheaper to resize preemptively before performance degrades noticeably than to suffer through a long stretch of increasingly slow operations and then do one big resize at the very end.

When a resize is actually triggered, the implementation allocates a new array that is typically larger — almost universally, exactly twice the size of the previous one. It then takes every key-value pair from the old table, computes a new slot index for each one (using the same hash function but taking the modulo of the new, larger array size), and inserts it into the appropriate location in the new structure. In the chaining-based case this is straightforward: each pair either lands in the same index or moves to a different one, and it's appended to whatever list lives there. In the open-addressing case it's more delicate, since you need to re-probe until every entry has a valid final position in the new table. During this period of rebuilding, depending on the implementation, you either pause all reads and writes (the simplest and most common approach), or you use some sort of concurrent rehashing scheme where readers keep working against a combination of the old and new structures while a background step migrates entries gradually. Either way, after the resize completes, you switch your reference to the new table, deallocate the old one, and everything continues from there. Because doubling the capacity means the hash values now have twice as many distinct indices to distribute across, the effective load drops immediately, collision pressure eases for a while, and the next resize won't need to be triggered until roughly twice as many more entries have accumulated.
